package_info.why_malicious: The entire package is considered malicious because an attacker can take over a previously popular repository namespace and publish arbitrary code under the original trusted name, poisoning the supply chain for all downstream users who depend on the original repository. This enables the attacker to distribute malicious code to unsuspecting users who trust the original package source.

execution_context.file_location: main.go (or equivalent entrypoint in hijacked repo)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code accesses the SECRET_TOKEN environment variable, sends its value to a hardcoded external domain via HTTPS POST, resulting in credential exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code reads a sensitive environment variable (SECRET_TOKEN) and transmits its value to an attacker-controlled server without user knowledge or consent, which is a clear indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate open-source packages do not access or exfiltrate secrets or environment variables during import or build time, especially to untrusted external domains.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or crash reporting libraries may send anonymized usage data, but they do not transmit secrets or tokens, and such behavior is always disclosed and opt-in.
key_indicators: Access to environment variables unrelated to package functionality
Hardcoded external domain (https://attacker.com/exfil) for data exfiltration
Network activity initiated at import/build time
Use of init() function to trigger code execution automatically

execution_context.file_location: main.go or supporting files in hijacked repo

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At import-time, the code retrieves the HOSTNAME environment variable and sends it as a query parameter to an attacker-controlled server via HTTP GET, enabling victim enumeration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code collects system information (hostname) and sends it to an external server controlled by the attacker, without user consent or legitimate purpose.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not transmit hostnames or system information to third parties during import or build time, especially without explicit user disclosure.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some analytics libraries may collect anonymized usage data, but not at import-time and not without user disclosure or opt-in.
key_indicators: Network requests to untrusted or attacker-controlled domains (https://attacker.com/ping)
Use of environment variables (HOSTNAME) in network requests
Automatic execution via init() at import/build time

attack_chain.action: Attacker claims a previously retired GitHub namespace by pre-creating a repository and then renaming the account to match the original package's namespace.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to publish code under a trusted package name, impersonating the original maintainer.

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes a malicious version of the package in the hijacked repository, embedding code that exfiltrates secrets and system information.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is now available under the original trusted import path, making it indistinguishable from the legitimate package for downstream users.

attack_chain.action: Victims import or build the package, triggering execution of malicious code that exfiltrates sensitive data and beacons system information.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive environment variables and enumeration of victim systems, enabling further targeted attacks.

behavioral_signatures: Unexpected network requests initiated during package import or build time
Access to environment variables or system information (e.g., SECRET_TOKEN, HOSTNAME) in package initialization code
Presence of code that references external, non-official domains within package source files
Use of init() functions or equivalent to trigger automatic execution upon import
file_indicators: main.go or equivalent entrypoint containing network or exfiltration logic
References to attacker-controlled domains (e.g., attacker.com) in source code
Presence of code accessing sensitive environment variables in initialization routines
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to domains not associated with the legitimate package maintainer (e.g., attacker.com)
Beaconing or exfiltration to new or suspicious domains after package update
Network traffic to hardcoded endpoints during build or import processes
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages whose repository ownership or namespace has changed unexpectedly, especially if the repository was previously retired or renamed. Scan imported packages for code that accesses environment variables or makes network requests at import/build time, particularly within init() or equivalent initialization functions. Flag any package that sends data to domains not previously associated with the package. Use tools like ChainJacking to identify dependencies vulnerable to repository hijacking. Implement static and dynamic analysis to detect unauthorized network activity and environment variable access during package initialization.
